summary:
Joseph Nelson, Co-founder/CEO of Roboflow, presents paint.wtf, a viral AI Pictionary game combining GPT-3-generated prompts, a browser-based MS Paint-like drawing canvas, and OpenAI's CLIP model for judging. CLIP evaluates drawings by computing cosine similarity between the text embedding of the prompt and the image embedding of the user's drawing; whichever embedding is most similar ranks highest on a Supabase-powered leaderboard. In its first week, paint.wtf attracted 120,000 players, peaked at 7 requests per second, and accumulated over 200,000 submissions after going viral on Reddit and Hacker News. The original app was built in 48 hours.

Nelson demonstrates building an MVP live in approximately 5 minutes using fewer than 50 lines of Python. The stack includes OpenCV (cv2), Roboflow's open-source inference server (pip install inference), and supervision for visualization. He first shows a Rock Paper Scissors object detection model from Roboflow Universe (50,000+ pre-trained models), then switches to CLIP for text and image embedding comparison. CLIP similarity scores ranged from approximately 13% to 45%, which the app scaled to 0-100 for display.

Key lessons emerged from operating the app at scale. First, CLIP can read text—users discovered that writing the prompt as text in their drawings boosted similarity scores, with one user ranking 81 out of 10,187 by simply writing "raccoon driving a tractor." Roboflow solved this by using CLIP to self-moderate: if an image was more similar to handwriting than the prompt, it was penalized. Second, CLIP similarity scores are conservative (8%–48% across 20,000+ submissions), requiring rescaling for display. Third, strangers on the internet submitted unexpected and NSFW content; Roboflow again used CLIP for moderation, blocking images more similar to NSFW content than the prompt. This created a cat-and-mouse game as users drew the prompt while sneaking in other content. Finally, Roboflow's inference server simplified deployment, incorporating learnings from serving hundreds of millions of API calls and maximizing throughput on target hardware, running at 15 FPS on an M1 Mac.

sections.title: Introduction to paint.wtf
sections.summary: Nelson introduces paint.wtf as an AI Pictionary game where GPT-3 generates prompts, users draw in a browser, and CLIP judges drawings by comparing text and image embeddings. It had 120,000 players in its first week, peaked at 7 requests per second, and went viral on Reddit and Hacker News.

sections.title: Site demo and example prompts
sections.summary: Nelson demos the live site showing user drawings for prompts like 'raccoon driving a tractor' (10,000 submissions) and 'world's most fabulous monster' (30,000 submissions). He highlights how CLIP understands low-fidelity drawings and abstract concepts like 'a bumblebee that loves capitalism,' representing open-set understanding.

sections.title: How the app works conceptually
sections.summary: Nelson explains the app architecture: GPT generates a prompt, users draw, CLIP produces text and image embeddings, and cosine similarity determines the winner. The leaderboard was powered by Supabase. Winning is equivalent to minimizing the distance between the prompt and drawing embeddings.

sections.title: Live coding demo
sections.summary: Nelson live-codes an MVP using OpenCV, Roboflow's inference server, and supervision. He first demos a Rock Paper Scissors object detection model from Roboflow Universe, then switches to CLIP, creating text embeddings for a prompt and preparing image similarity scoring via webcam. He notes CLIP similarities ranged from ~13% to 45% and scales them to 0-100.

sections.title: Live volunteer demo with Nat and swix
sections.summary: Nelson invites volunteers Nat and swix to draw 'a gorilla gardening with grapes' and compares their drawings against CLIP's similarity scoring via webcam. Swix attempts a prompt injection attack. Nelson also draws his own submission. Nat wins a Lenny mascot from Roboflow.

sections.title: Transition to lessons
sections.summary: Nelson transitions to sharing lessons learned from the trials and tribulations of putting an image-submission app on the internet, noting that CLIP can be tricked by users writing words in their drawings. The code is available via pip install inference with examples on GitHub.

sections.title: Lessons: CLIP text reading, scoring, and content moderation
sections.summary: Nelson shares key lessons. First, CLIP can read text—users wrote prompts as text to game scores, with one ranking 81 of 10,187. The fix used CLIP to self-moderate by penalizing images more similar to handwriting than the prompt. Second, CLIP similarities are conservative (8%-48% across 20,000+ submissions), requiring rescaling. Third, strangers submitted NSFW content, moderated by comparing CLIP similarity to NSFW vs. prompt text. This created a cat-and-mouse game. Finally, Roboflow's inference server simplifies deployment, leveraging learnings from hundreds of millions of API calls, running at 15 FPS on an M1 Mac. Nelson thanks the volunteers and closes.
